question.text: Who do Minnesota's traffic laws apply to?

answer.text: Minnesota's traffic laws cover every person who drives on a public road anywhere in the state.

teaching.text: Every person driving on any public road in Minnesota is covered by the state's traffic laws. Remember: Every driver, every public road.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Minnesota's traffic laws cover every person who drives on a public road anywhere in the state.

question.text: When may you leave the right side of a wide road?

answer.text: On roads of sufficient width you keep to the right side unless you are passing a vehicle going your way, the right side is closed for construction or repair, the road has three marked lanes, signs make it one-way, or you are moving over for a stopped authorized vehicle under the Move Over Law.

teaching.text: Stay on the right side of a wide road unless passing, the right side is closed, there are three marked lanes, it is one-way, or you are moving over. Remember: Keep right unless an exception.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On roads of sufficient width you keep to the right side unless you are passing a vehicle going your way, the right side is closed for construction or repair, the road has three marked lanes, signs make it one-way, or you are moving over for a stopped authorized vehicle under the Move Over Law.

question.text: What does the basic speed law require?

answer.text: Under the basic speed law your speed must be reasonable for the current weather, traffic and road conditions, and the posted limit is the highest speed allowed on that road.

teaching.text: Choose a speed that suits the weather, traffic and road, and treat the posted limit as the most you may ever drive. Remember: Reasonable for conditions, never over.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under the basic speed law your speed must be reasonable for the current weather, traffic and road conditions, and the posted limit is the highest speed allowed on that road.

question.text: Is it legal to drive below a posted minimum speed in normal conditions?

answer.text: Where a minimum speed limit is posted, driving below it under normal conditions is illegal.

teaching.text: A posted minimum speed is a real limit, so going slower than it in normal conditions breaks the law. Remember: Minimums are limits too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where a minimum speed limit is posted, driving below it under normal conditions is illegal.

question.text: What is the default speed limit in an alley?

answer.text: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit in an alley under ideal conditions is ten miles per hour

teaching.text: With no signs posted, alleys have a ten miles per hour limit under ideal conditions. Remember: Alleys crawl at ten.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit in an alley under ideal conditions is ten miles per hour

question.text: What is the default speed limit on urban or town roads?

answer.text: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit on urban or town roads under ideal conditions is thirty miles per hour

teaching.text: Urban and town roads default to thirty miles per hour under ideal conditions unless signs say otherwise. Remember: Town roads thirty.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit on urban or town roads under ideal conditions is thirty miles per hour

question.text: What is the default speed limit where no other default applies?

answer.text: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit under ideal conditions is fifty-five miles per hour in every location not otherwise listed.

teaching.text: Anywhere without another listed default, the limit is fifty-five miles per hour under ideal conditions. Remember: Everywhere else fifty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit under ideal conditions is fifty-five miles per hour in every location not otherwise listed.

question.text: What must you do in school zones and work zones?

answer.text: In a school zone you must slow down when children are present, and in a work or construction zone you must slow down and drive carefully.

teaching.text: Slow down in a school zone whenever children are present, and slow down and take care in work or construction zones. Remember: Kids present or crews: slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a school zone you must slow down when children are present, and in a work or construction zone you must slow down and drive carefully.

question.text: What are the three default speed limits under ideal conditions?

answer.text: The three default limits under ideal conditions are ten miles per hour in alleys, thirty miles per hour on urban or town roads and fifty-five miles per hour everywhere else, and posted signs override all three.

teaching.text: Remember the three defaults as a set: ten in alleys, thirty on town roads, fifty-five elsewhere, with signs overriding them. Remember: Ten, thirty, fifty-five.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The three default limits under ideal conditions are ten miles per hour in alleys, thirty miles per hour on urban or town roads and fifty-five miles per hour everywhere else, and posted signs override all three.

question.text: When may you exceed the limit by ten miles per hour?

answer.text: On two-lane highways posted at fifty-five miles per hour or higher you may go up to ten miles per hour over the limit, but only while lawfully passing another vehicle.

teaching.text: The ten-over allowance only covers a lawful pass on a two-lane highway posted at fifty-five or higher. Remember: Passing on fast two-lanes only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On two-lane highways posted at fifty-five miles per hour or higher you may go up to ten miles per hour over the limit, but only while lawfully passing another vehicle.

question.text: How does driving faster affect crash risk?

answer.text: Driving faster shortens the time you have to react, raises the odds of a crash and makes serious injury or death in a crash more likely.

teaching.text: Speed cuts the time you have to react and makes crashes, serious injuries and deaths more likely. Remember: Faster means less reaction time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving faster shortens the time you have to react, raises the odds of a crash and makes serious injury or death in a crash more likely.

question.text: What happens to your right-of-way if you reach an intersection at an unlawful speed?

answer.text: A driver who reaches an intersection at an unlawful speed gives up the right-of-way they would have had at a lawful speed.

teaching.text: Reach an intersection at an unlawful speed and you lose the right-of-way a lawful speed would have given you. Remember: Speeders forfeit the right-of-way.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver who reaches an intersection at an unlawful speed gives up the right-of-way they would have had at a lawful speed.

question.text: When do extra speeding fines apply?

answer.text: Speeding can bring a fine, and extra fines apply when you drive twenty miles per hour or more above the posted limit.

teaching.text: Speeding can bring a fine, and going twenty or more over the posted limit adds extra fines. Remember: Twenty over costs extra.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speeding can bring a fine, and extra fines apply when you drive twenty miles per hour or more above the posted limit.

question.text: What happens if you drive faster than one hundred miles per hour?

answer.text: Driving faster than one hundred miles per hour leads to revocation of your driving privileges for at least six months.

teaching.text: Driving over one hundred miles per hour means losing your driving privileges for at least six months. Remember: Triple digits, lose license.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving faster than one hundred miles per hour leads to revocation of your driving privileges for at least six months.

question.text: What must you do when passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights?

answer.text: You must slow down when approaching or passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing emergency lights, and breaking this rule adds a surcharge of at least twenty-five dollars to the speeding fine.

teaching.text: Slow down near a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights, or a surcharge of at least twenty-five dollars is added to your fine. Remember: Slow down or pay surcharge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You must slow down when approaching or passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing emergency lights, and breaking this rule adds a surcharge of at least twenty-five dollars to the speeding fine.

question.text: How do the penalties for twenty over and for over one hundred differ?

answer.text: Going twenty miles per hour or more over the limit adds extra fines, while going over one hundred miles per hour costs your driving privileges for at least six months.

teaching.text: Twenty or more over means extra fines, while over one hundred means revocation for at least six months. Remember: Twenty fines, hundred revokes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Going twenty miles per hour or more over the limit adds extra fines, while going over one hundred miles per hour costs your driving privileges for at least six months.

question.text: What does higher speed do to your field of vision?

answer.text: Higher speed narrows your field of vision as well as raising the risk of a crash.

teaching.text: The faster you go, the narrower your field of vision becomes, on top of the higher crash risk. Remember: Speed shrinks what you see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Higher speed narrows your field of vision as well as raising the risk of a crash.

question.text: Which roadway hazards call for reducing speed?

answer.text: Watch for flag persons, pedestrians, barricades, flares or reflectors in the roadway and reduce speed for them, as well as in bad weather and on poor road surfaces.

teaching.text: Ease off for flag persons, pedestrians, barricades, flares or reflectors, and in bad weather or on poor surfaces. Remember: Flaggers, walkers, flares: slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch for flag persons, pedestrians, barricades, flares or reflectors in the roadway and reduce speed for them, as well as in bad weather and on poor road surfaces.

question.text: Which road shapes and features call for slower speeds?

answer.text: Reduce speed on narrow or winding roads and as you near a curve, the top of a hill or a railroad crossing.

teaching.text: Narrow or winding roads, curves, hilltops and railroad crossings all call for a slower speed. Remember: Curves, hills, crossings: ease off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reduce speed on narrow or winding roads and as you near a curve, the top of a hill or a railroad crossing.

question.text: Why slow down on gravel or dirt roads?

answer.text: On gravel or dirt roads slow down, because stopping takes longer and the vehicle skids more easily in a turn.

teaching.text: On gravel or dirt, stopping takes longer and turns can turn into skids, so slow down. Remember: Loose roads, longer stops.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On gravel or dirt roads slow down, because stopping takes longer and the vehicle skids more easily in a turn.

question.text: What special rules may apply on bridges?

answer.text: Bridges may carry their own speed limits and No Passing signs, and you must watch for and obey them.

teaching.text: Bridges can post their own speed limits and No Passing signs, and those must be obeyed. Remember: Bridges post their own rules.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bridges may carry their own speed limits and No Passing signs, and you must watch for and obey them.

question.text: How far before a turn must you signal?

answer.text: Turn on your signal at least one hundred feet before you turn, and keep it on until the turn or lane change is finished.

teaching.text: Switch your signal on at least one hundred feet before the turn and leave it on until the move is complete. Remember: Signal a hundred feet early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn on your signal at least one hundred feet before you turn, and keep it on until the turn or lane change is finished.

question.text: When may you use hand and arm signals?

answer.text: In daylight you may use hand and arm signals along with or in place of turn signals, but not at night or in a vehicle that hides your hand from other drivers.

teaching.text: In daylight you may signal with your hand and arm, alone or with turn signals, but never at night or when your arm cannot be seen. Remember: Hand signals by daylight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In daylight you may use hand and arm signals along with or in place of turn signals, but not at night or in a vehicle that hides your hand from other drivers.

question.text: May you use hand signals at night?

answer.text: Hand and arm signals are a daylight option only; at night, or when your vehicle hides your arm, rely on the turn signals.

teaching.text: Hand and arm signals are a daylight tool only; at night or with a hidden arm, use the turn signals. Remember: Night means turn signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand and arm signals are a daylight option only; at night, or when your vehicle hides your arm, rely on the turn signals.

question.text: Does a lane exist if it is not marked?

answer.text: A traffic lane exists whether or not it is marked, and you must stay inside one lane without weaving or straddling the markings.

teaching.text: Lanes are there whether or not they are painted, so keep within one lane without weaving or straddling lines. Remember: Lanes exist without lines.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A traffic lane exists whether or not it is marked, and you must stay inside one lane without weaving or straddling the markings.

question.text: What should you do before changing lanes?

answer.text: Before changing lanes make sure there is room beside, behind and ahead of you, and turn your head to check the new lane instead of relying only on mirrors.

teaching.text: Before a lane change, check for room beside, behind and ahead, and turn your head rather than trusting only your mirrors. Remember: Space all around, turn head.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before changing lanes make sure there is room beside, behind and ahead of you, and turn your head to check the new lane instead of relying only on mirrors.

question.text: What are blind spots and what creates them?

answer.text: Blind spots are areas your mirrors cannot show; the vehicle's design and roof pillars decide where they are, and a dirty windshield or glare can add temporary ones.

teaching.text: Your mirrors cannot show your blind spots, which come from the vehicle's design and roof pillars, and dirt or glare can add more. Remember: Pillars and glare hide cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Blind spots are areas your mirrors cannot show; the vehicle's design and roof pillars decide where they are, and a dirty windshield or glare can add temporary ones.

question.text: Whose blind spots should you avoid driving in?

answer.text: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, and pay special attention to them near commercial vehicles.

teaching.text: Do not linger in another driver's blind spot, and be especially careful around commercial vehicles. Remember: Don't linger in blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, and pay special attention to them near commercial vehicles.

question.text: How do you avoid improper turns?

answer.text: Improper turns cause many crashes, so move into the correct lane well before the point where you will turn.

teaching.text: Many crashes come from improper turns, so move into the right lane well before you reach the turn. Remember: Right lane early, then turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Improper turns cause many crashes, so move into the correct lane well before the point where you will turn.

question.text: What should you never do when turning?

answer.text: Never make a sudden turn from the wrong lane, watch for traffic or obstacles on the road you are entering, and always end the turn in the correct lane.

teaching.text: Never swing into a turn from the wrong lane, check the road you are entering, and finish in the correct lane. Remember: No sudden wrong-lane turns.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never make a sudden turn from the wrong lane, watch for traffic or obstacles on the road you are entering, and always end the turn in the correct lane.

question.text: How should your wheels point while you wait to turn?

answer.text: While you wait to turn, keep the wheels pointed straight and your foot on the brake so a rear-end hit is less likely to shove you into oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Keep the wheels straight and your foot on the brake while waiting, so a rear-end hit does not push you into oncoming traffic. Remember: Wheels straight while waiting.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: While you wait to turn, keep the wheels pointed straight and your foot on the brake so a rear-end hit is less likely to shove you into oncoming traffic.

question.text: Where do you wait when turning left on green with oncoming traffic?

answer.text: When waiting to turn left on a green light with traffic coming toward you, pull into the intersection until your body lines up with the curb line, and you may only get to turn once the light turns yellow.

teaching.text: Turning left on green with traffic coming, pull in until your body lines up with the curb line, and you may only turn when the light goes yellow. Remember: Body even with curb line.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When waiting to turn left on a green light with traffic coming toward you, pull into the intersection until your body lines up with the curb line, and you may only get to turn once the light turns yellow.

question.text: What should you do when the car ahead signals a left turn?

answer.text: If the car ahead is signaling a left turn, slow down and get ready to stop.

teaching.text: When the car in front signals a left turn, slow down and be ready to stop. Remember: Left signal ahead: ease up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the car ahead is signaling a left turn, slow down and get ready to stop.

question.text: How do you make a left turn and where do you finish?

answer.text: For a left turn, check behind you and signal, move into the lane nearest the center line, or just right of the road's center if lanes are unmarked, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the first lane to the right of the center line.

teaching.text: For a left turn, signal, move to the lane nearest the center line, look both ways, yield if needed and finish just right of the center line. Remember: Center lane in, right of center.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a left turn, check behind you and signal, move into the lane nearest the center line, or just right of the road's center if lanes are unmarked, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the first lane to the right of the center line.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Center lane in, right of center

question.text: How do you make a right turn and where do you finish?

answer.text: For a right turn, check behind you and signal, move close to the right curb, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the lane next to the curb.

teaching.text: For a right turn, signal, move close to the right curb, look both ways, yield if needed and finish in the curb lane. Remember: Hug the curb, finish curbside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: For a right turn, check behind you and signal, move close to the right curb, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the lane next to the curb.

question.text: Where do left and right turns finish, and how do you steer?

answer.text: A left turn ends in the first lane to the right of the center line, while a right turn ends in the lane next to the curb, and both use hand-over-hand steering.

teaching.text: Left turns end in the first lane right of the center line, right turns in the curb lane, both using hand-over-hand steering. Remember: Left near center, right by curb.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A left turn ends in the first lane to the right of the center line, while a right turn ends in the lane next to the curb, and both use hand-over-hand steering.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Left near center, right by curb

question.text: How do you drive through multiple turn lanes?

answer.text: Where signs or lane markings show two or more turning lanes, stay in your own lane all the way through the turn.

teaching.text: When signs or markings show two or more turn lanes, stay in your own lane from start to finish. Remember: Stay in your turn lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where signs or lane markings show two or more turning lanes, stay in your own lane all the way through the turn.

question.text: When may you turn right on a red light?

answer.text: Many intersections allow a right turn on red after a complete stop in the correct lane, unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, and only after checking every direction for pedestrians and traffic.

teaching.text: A right on red is allowed at many intersections after a full stop in the correct lane, unless a sign forbids it, once the way is clear. Remember: Stop, look, then right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Many intersections allow a right turn on red after a complete stop in the correct lane, unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, and only after checking every direction for pedestrians and traffic.

question.text: When is a left turn on red allowed?

answer.text: A left turn on red is allowed in certain cases only when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a complete stop and once the intersection is clear.

teaching.text: A left on red is only possible from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a full stop with the intersection clear. Remember: One-way onto one-way only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A left turn on red is allowed in certain cases only when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a complete stop and once the intersection is clear.

question.text: How do the rules for right on red and left on red differ?

answer.text: A right turn on red is allowed at many intersections, but a left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, and both need a complete stop first.

teaching.text: Right on red is common, but left on red needs one-way streets on both sides, and both begin with a complete stop. Remember: Right often, left one-way only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A right turn on red is allowed at many intersections, but a left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, and both need a complete stop first.

question.text: What should you watch for when turning right on red?

answer.text: When you turn right on red, watch for oncoming drivers turning left in front of you, since their green arrow may come on before your light turns green.

teaching.text: Turning right on red, watch for oncoming drivers turning left, because their green arrow may come before your green light. Remember: Watch oncoming green arrows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you turn right on red, watch for oncoming drivers turning left in front of you, since their green arrow may come on before your light turns green.

question.text: What must you do whenever you turn on a red light?

answer.text: Whenever you turn on a red light, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and where a No Turn on Red sign is posted, wait for the green light.

teaching.text: Any turn on red means yielding to traffic and pedestrians, and a No Turn on Red sign means waiting for green. Remember: Yield first, obey no-turn signs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Whenever you turn on a red light, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and where a No Turn on Red sign is posted, wait for the green light.

question.text: Why are roundabouts used instead of four-way stops?

answer.text: Roundabouts are built to move traffic better and to make intersections safer than ordinary four-way stops.

teaching.text: Roundabouts are designed to keep traffic moving and to be safer than ordinary four-way stops. Remember: Smoother flow, safer intersections.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Roundabouts are built to move traffic better and to make intersections safer than ordinary four-way stops.

question.text: What should you do as you approach a roundabout?

answer.text: As you approach a roundabout, slow down, pick your lane before entering if it has more than one lane, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists crossing, and watch for signs or markings that require or forbid certain moves.

teaching.text: Approaching a roundabout, slow down, choose your lane before entering, yield to crossing pedestrians and bicyclists and follow the signs. Remember: Slow, pick lane, yield walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: As you approach a roundabout, slow down, pick your lane before entering if it has more than one lane, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists crossing, and watch for signs or markings that require or forbid certain moves.

question.text: When may you enter a roundabout?

answer.text: Enter a roundabout only after yielding to vehicles already circulating and after all traffic coming from your left has cleared.

teaching.text: Enter only after traffic already circling, and everything coming from your left, has gone by. Remember: Yield to circulating traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Enter a roundabout only after yielding to vehicles already circulating and after all traffic coming from your left has cleared.

question.text: How do you drive once inside a roundabout?

answer.text: Inside a roundabout drive counterclockwise to your exit and never stop, pass or change lanes.

teaching.text: Travel counterclockwise to your exit, and never stop, pass or change lanes inside the roundabout. Remember: Counterclockwise, no stops or swaps.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Inside a roundabout drive counterclockwise to your exit and never stop, pass or change lanes.

question.text: What do you do if an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout?

answer.text: If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, leave the roundabout right away and then pull over.

teaching.text: If an emergency vehicle comes while you are in a roundabout, exit first and then pull over. Remember: Exit first, then pull over.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, leave the roundabout right away and then pull over.

question.text: Which vehicles may leave their lane in a roundabout?

answer.text: Any combination vehicle, or a vehicle over forty feet long or more than ten feet wide, may leave its lane as needed to get through a roundabout while watching other traffic.

teaching.text: Combination vehicles and vehicles over forty feet long or ten feet wide may use more than their lane in a roundabout. Remember: Big rigs may swing wide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Any combination vehicle, or a vehicle over forty feet long or more than ten feet wide, may leave its lane as needed to get through a roundabout while watching other traffic.

question.text: Who yields when two large vehicles go through a multi-lane roundabout together?

answer.text: Entering cars yield to cars already in the roundabout, but when two large vehicles go through a multi-lane roundabout side by side, the driver on the right yields to the one on the left, slowing or stopping if needed.

teaching.text: Entering drivers yield to circulating traffic, and when two large vehicles are side by side, the one on the right yields to the left. Remember: Right big rig yields left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Entering cars yield to cars already in the roundabout, but when two large vehicles go through a multi-lane roundabout side by side, the driver on the right yields to the one on the left, slowing or stopping if needed.

question.text: Why are J-turns built on divided highways?

answer.text: J-turns exist to cut deaths and injuries from broadside crashes on four-lane divided highways.

teaching.text: J-turns replace dangerous crossings to cut deaths and injuries from broadside crashes on four-lane divided highways. Remember: Fewer broadside crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: J-turns exist to cut deaths and injuries from broadside crashes on four-lane divided highways.

question.text: How do you cross or turn left using a J-turn?

answer.text: At a J-turn every side-street driver turns right; to cross or go left you stop completely, turn right onto the highway, move into the marked left-turn lane at the median opening and make a U-turn.

teaching.text: At a J-turn, turn right, move into the left-turn lane at the median opening and make a U-turn to cross or go left. Remember: Right, merge left, U-turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a J-turn every side-street driver turns right; to cross or go left you stop completely, turn right onto the highway, move into the marked left-turn lane at the median opening and make a U-turn.

question.text: May you cross both lanes in one motion at a J-turn?

answer.text: During the right turn at a J-turn you may cross both lanes into the left-turn lane in a single motion when it is safe, which shortens your time in the through lanes.

teaching.text: When it is safe, the right turn at a J-turn may cross both lanes straight into the left-turn lane. Remember: Both lanes at once if safe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: During the right turn at a J-turn you may cross both lanes into the left-turn lane in a single motion when it is safe, which shortens your time in the through lanes.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Both lanes at once if safe

question.text: What must you do when finishing the U-turn at a J-turn?

answer.text: When finishing the U-turn at a J-turn you must yield to oncoming traffic, stopping if needed, before entering the through lanes.

teaching.text: Finishing the U-turn at a J-turn, yield to oncoming traffic and stop if needed before joining the through lanes. Remember: Yield before the through lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When finishing the U-turn at a J-turn you must yield to oncoming traffic, stopping if needed, before entering the through lanes.

question.text: How may you cross a rural divided highway with a wide median?

answer.text: When a rural divided highway has enough room between its roadways, you may cross one half, wait in the middle to the right of center, and cross the second half when it is safe.

teaching.text: With enough median space on a rural divided highway, cross one half, wait right of center, then cross the rest. Remember: Cross half, wait, cross half.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a rural divided highway has enough room between its roadways, you may cross one half, wait in the middle to the right of center, and cross the second half when it is safe.

question.text: What extra care does turning left onto a divided highway need?

answer.text: Turning left onto a divided highway follows the same steps as crossing it, and you must leave enough room that you do not slow oncoming traffic while you speed up.

teaching.text: Turning left onto a divided highway uses the same steps as crossing, leaving enough room not to slow oncoming traffic. Remember: Room to speed up safely.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turning left onto a divided highway follows the same steps as crossing it, and you must leave enough room that you do not slow oncoming traffic while you speed up.

question.text: When is a U-turn allowed?

answer.text: A U-turn reverses your direction with a half-circle turn, is allowed only when it will not disrupt other traffic, and is forbidden wherever a No U-Turn sign is posted.

teaching.text: A U-turn is only allowed when it will not disrupt traffic, and never where a No U-Turn sign is posted. Remember: U-turn only without disruption.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A U-turn reverses your direction with a half-circle turn, is allowed only when it will not disrupt other traffic, and is forbidden wherever a No U-Turn sign is posted.

question.text: Where are U-turns banned?

answer.text: U-turns are banned on interstate freeways, and also near hilltops or on curves where drivers coming toward you could not see you from one thousand feet away.

teaching.text: No U-turns on interstate freeways, or near hilltops and curves where oncoming drivers could not see you from one thousand feet. Remember: No U-turns on freeways or blind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: U-turns are banned on interstate freeways, and also near hilltops or on curves where drivers coming toward you could not see you from one thousand feet away.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: No U-turns on freeways or blind

question.text: How may you make a U-turn on a road with two or more lanes your way?

answer.text: On a roadway with two or more lanes in your direction, you may swing into the farthest lane and briefly use the shoulder to finish a U-turn when needed.

teaching.text: With two or more lanes your way, you may use the farthest lane and briefly the shoulder to finish a U-turn. Remember: Far lane plus shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a roadway with two or more lanes in your direction, you may swing into the farthest lane and briefly use the shoulder to finish a U-turn when needed.

question.text: Where must a slow driver stay on a road with one lane each way?

answer.text: With only one lane in your direction, a driver going slowly enough to create a hazard must stay as close as possible to the right curb or road edge.

teaching.text: On a road with one lane your way, a driver slow enough to be a hazard must keep close to the right edge. Remember: Slow means hug the right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With only one lane in your direction, a driver going slowly enough to create a hazard must stay as close as possible to the right curb or road edge.

question.text: Which lane should you use on a highway with several lanes your way?

answer.text: On highways with more than one lane in your direction, use the right-hand lane when one is available, and leave the left-most lane to let another vehicle pass when practical.

teaching.text: On multi-lane highways, use the right-hand lane when available and leave the left lane so others can pass. Remember: Keep right, let others pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On highways with more than one lane in your direction, use the right-hand lane when one is available, and leave the left-most lane to let another vehicle pass when practical.

question.text: When may you use a lane other than the right-hand lane?

answer.text: You may use a lane other than the right-hand lane when passing, preparing a left turn at an intersection or into a driveway, preparing a left-side exit from an expressway, freeway or interstate, driving an authorized emergency vehicle, or following a traffic control device, a peace officer or work zone directions.

teaching.text: You may use another lane to pass, to prepare a left turn or left exit, in an emergency vehicle, or when directed by signs, officers or work zones. Remember: Pass, turn, exit, emergency, directed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You may use a lane other than the right-hand lane when passing, preparing a left turn at an intersection or into a driveway, preparing a left-side exit from an expressway, freeway or interstate, driving an authorized emergency vehicle, or following a traffic control device, a peace officer or work zone directions.

question.text: What should you check before passing?

answer.text: Take extra care passing at night, in poor visibility or on slippery roads, and before passing make sure oncoming traffic is far enough away and that nobody behind you is starting to pass.

teaching.text: Pass with extra care at night, in poor visibility or on slippery roads, after checking oncoming traffic and the drivers behind you. Remember: Gap ahead, nobody behind passing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Take extra care passing at night, in poor visibility or on slippery roads, and before passing make sure oncoming traffic is far enough away and that nobody behind you is starting to pass.

question.text: How do you signal and return when passing?

answer.text: Signal left before moving out to pass and signal right after passing, then return to the right lane once the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror.

teaching.text: Signal left to pull out, signal right before returning, and return once the whole passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror. Remember: Left out, right back, mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal left before moving out to pass and signal right after passing, then return to the right lane once the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror.

question.text: How soon must you be back in your lane after passing?

answer.text: After passing you must be back on the right side of the road before you come within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle.

teaching.text: Get back to the right side before you come within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle. Remember: Back before a hundred feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After passing you must be back on the right side of the road before you come within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle.

question.text: Which two passing rules both use one hundred feet?

answer.text: On the passing page one hundred feet appears twice: you must be back in the right lane before you are within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle, and you may not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection, underpass, tunnel or railroad crossing.

teaching.text: One hundred feet shows up twice: the gap to oncoming traffic when you return, and the no-passing zone near crossings and tunnels. Remember: Two hundreds on passing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On the passing page one hundred feet appears twice: you must be back in the right lane before you are within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle, and you may not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection, underpass, tunnel or railroad crossing.

question.text: Where may you not pass?

answer.text: You may not pass where a No Passing Zone sign is posted or where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, and double solid yellow lines forbid passing in both directions.

teaching.text: No passing at a No Passing Zone sign or with solid yellow on your side, and double solid yellow bans both directions. Remember: Solid yellow, sign: no pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You may not pass where a No Passing Zone sign is posted or where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, and double solid yellow lines forbid passing in both directions.

question.text: How do single and double solid yellow lines differ for passing?

answer.text: A single solid yellow line on your side bans passing for you, while a double solid yellow line bans passing for drivers in both directions.

teaching.text: Solid yellow on your side stops your pass; double solid yellow stops everyone's. Remember: Single bans you, double both.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A single solid yellow line on your side bans passing for you, while a double solid yellow line bans passing for drivers in both directions.

question.text: How much clear road must you see ahead to pass on a hill or curve?

answer.text: Never pass on a hill or curve unless you can clearly see at least seven hundred feet of road ahead.

teaching.text: On a hill or curve, pass only if you can clearly see at least seven hundred feet of road ahead. Remember: Seven hundred feet to pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never pass on a hill or curve unless you can clearly see at least seven hundred feet of road ahead.

question.text: Near which places is passing not allowed?

answer.text: Passing is not allowed within one hundred feet of an intersection, an underpass, a tunnel or a railroad crossing.

teaching.text: Never pass within one hundred feet of an intersection, an underpass, a tunnel or a railroad crossing. Remember: Crossings, tunnels, underpasses: no pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing is not allowed within one hundred feet of an intersection, an underpass, a tunnel or a railroad crossing.

question.text: What should you do when another driver is passing you?

answer.text: Do not pass when you are about to meet an oncoming vehicle, and when someone is passing you, stay in your lane and do not speed up.

teaching.text: Do not pass when an oncoming vehicle is near, and when you are being passed, hold your lane and do not speed up. Remember: Hold lane, hold speed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not pass when you are about to meet an oncoming vehicle, and when someone is passing you, stay in your lane and do not speed up.

question.text: When may you pass on the right?

answer.text: You may pass on the right only when it is safe and the vehicle ahead is turning or about to turn left, or the road has room for two or more lanes of moving traffic each way, or it is a one-way road wide enough for two or more lanes with nothing in the way.

teaching.text: Passing on the right is only allowed when safe and the car ahead is turning left, or on roads wide enough for two or more lanes each way. Remember: Right pass only when allowed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You may pass on the right only when it is safe and the vehicle ahead is turning or about to turn left, or the road has room for two or more lanes of moving traffic each way, or it is a one-way road wide enough for two or more lanes with nothing in the way.

question.text: May you use the shoulder or a bike lane to pass on the right?

answer.text: A pass on the right must stay on the main roadway: using a bike lane, the shoulder or the unpaved edge to get around a vehicle is not allowed.

teaching.text: Never use the shoulder, a bike lane or the unpaved edge to pass someone on the right. Remember: Stay on the pavement.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A pass on the right must stay on the main roadway: using a bike lane, the shoulder or the unpaved edge to get around a vehicle is not allowed.

question.text: May you back up on a freeway or expressway?

answer.text: Backing up on freeways or expressways is not allowed except for emergency vehicles on duty, and backing on public roads can lead to a reckless or careless driving charge.

teaching.text: Only on-duty emergency vehicles may back up on freeways or expressways, and backing on public roads can bring a reckless or careless driving charge. Remember: Never reverse on freeways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Backing up on freeways or expressways is not allowed except for emergency vehicles on duty, and backing on public roads can lead to a reckless or careless driving charge.

question.text: How should you back out of a driveway?

answer.text: Leaving a driveway in reverse, back only into the closest lane and then pull forward, and never reverse into or across traffic lanes unless you are sure it is safe.

teaching.text: Backing out of a driveway, reverse only into the nearest lane and then drive forward, never across lanes unless it is clearly safe. Remember: Back to nearest lane only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Leaving a driveway in reverse, back only into the closest lane and then pull forward, and never reverse into or across traffic lanes unless you are sure it is safe.

hooks_spoken: Keep right on wide roads except for the listed reasons, and drive at a speed reasonable for conditions, never above the posted limit.

hooks_spoken: Twenty or more over brings extra fines, over one hundred brings at least six months' revocation, and skipping the emergency vehicle slow-down adds a surcharge.
Slow down for roadway hazards, curves, hills, crossings, gravel roads and bad weather.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of speeding penalties and slowing down. hooks_spoken: Signal at least one hundred feet before turning, and use hand signals only in daylight.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of signals, lanes and blind spots. Signal at least one hundred feet before turning, and use hand signals only in daylight. Stay inside one lane and turn your head to check blind spots before changing lanes. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Get into the correct lane early, wait with wheels straight, and finish left turns right of center and right turns by the curb.
Right on red is allowed at many intersections after a full stop, but left on red only from a one-way onto a one-way street.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of turns and turns on red. Get into the correct lane early, wait with wheels straight, and finish left turns right of center and right turns by the curb. hooks_spoken: In a roundabout, yield to traffic already circling, travel counterclockwise and never stop, pass or change lanes.
At a J-turn, turn right, move into the left-turn lane, make a U-turn and yield before entering the through lanes.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of roundabouts, J-turns and divided highways. In a roundabout, yield to traffic already circling, travel counterclockwise and never stop, pass or change lanes. At a J-turn, turn right, move into the left-turn lane, make a U-turn and yield before entering the through lanes. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: U-turns are banned on interstate freeways and where oncoming drivers could not see you from one thousand feet.
Use the right lane when available, except when passing, turning left, exiting left, driving an emergency vehicle or following directions.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of u-turns and right-lane travel. U-turns are banned on interstate freeways and where oncoming drivers could not see you from one thousand feet. Use the right lane when available, except when passing, turning left, exiting left, driving an emergency vehicle or following directions. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: See seven hundred feet ahead before passing on hills or curves, and be back in your lane before one hundred feet from oncoming traffic.
Solid yellow on your side bans your pass, double yellow bans everyone, and no passing within one hundred feet of crossings and intersections.
